Section 1.01 of the Credit Agreement is
hereby amended by adding the following definitions in the appropriate alphabetical order:
“Invoice
Restrictions” has the meaning set forth in the Monthly Factoring Report.
“Maintenance Liquidity”
means, as of any date of determination, (a) the sum as of such date of (x) the aggregate amount of the commitments under the Super-Priority Revolving Credit Facility (including the aggregate revolving commitments with respect to any
Permitted Euro Revolving Indebtedness) (or any Refinancing Indebtedness in respect thereof) minus (y) the aggregate principal amount of the outstanding revolving loans under the Super-Priority Revolving Credit Facility and any
outstanding revolving loans in respect of any Permitted Euro Revolving Indebtedness (or any Refinancing Indebtedness in respect thereof) and, in each case, the face amount of any letters of credit issued thereunder (less any reimbursed amounts)
plus (b) the “Adjustment to Liquidity” as set forth in the most recently delivered Monthly Factoring Report plus (c) unrestricted cash and Cash Equivalents of the Borrower and its Subsidiaries.

“Monthly Factoring Report” means a report substantially in
the form of Exhibit E or any other form approved by the Administrative Agent.

findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR includes only one definition (ir-definition:983a978297d0da9452f5da36) for 'Invoice Restrictions' but marks its sufficiency as PARTIAL and describes it as UNSUPPORTED.
findings.verifierReasoning: The source text states that 'Invoice Restrictions' is being added as a new defined term to Section 1.01 of the Credit Agreement, with a definition that reads 'has the meaning set forth in the Monthly Factoring Report.' The proposed IR correctly identifies this as PARTIAL/UNSUPPORTED because the meaning is not directly stated in this amendment but is instead delegated to an external document (the Monthly Factoring Report, defined in Exhibit E). However, the representation itself stops short of capturing what happens operationally: this term 'Invoice Restrictions' is used in Section 6.01(3) (which appears later in the amendment text) where it states: 'all of the invoices that meet the Invoice Restrictions are included in the Monthly Factoring Report.' This means Invoice Restrictions functions as a filter or criterion for which invoices must be included in reports. The proposed IR acknowledges the definition's incompleteness but does not capture the operational consequence: that compliance with covenant obligations (specifically monthly reporting) depends on applying these restrictions. The definition is marked PARTIAL, which is honest but leaves unrepresented the fact that this term gates a reporting obligation that itself has material compliance implications. This is not a hidden omission of the definition itself but rather an incomplete representation of its semantic role within the amendment's covenant structure.

findings.sourceEvidence: Section 2.05(2)(c): 'If, after giving effect to all mandatory prepayments of Term Loans to the extent required by Sections 2.05(2)(a), (b) and (d), the Borrower and its Subsidiaries has (i) unrestricted cash on hand as of the last day of any calendar month in an amount that is greater than $50 million, the Borrower shall, as soon as is reasonably practicable, but in any event no later than five (5) Business Days after the last day of such calendar month, prepay...'
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR contains only 1 rule with posture='N_A' and action=null, marked as PARTIAL sufficiency. It does not capture the mandatory prepayment mechanics introduced in the amendment.
findings.verifierReasoning: The operative text of the amendment includes Section 2(b), which amends Section 2.05(2)(c) with detailed mandatory prepayment mechanics tied to Maintenance Liquidity and unrestricted cash thresholds. Specifically: (i) if unrestricted cash exceeds $50 million, mandatory prepayment of revolving loans to bring it below $50 million; and (ii) if Maintenance Liquidity exceeds $115 million, mandatory prepayment of Term Loans to bring Maintenance Liquidity to $115 million or below. These are substantive operational rules that constrain the Borrower's use of cash and liquidity. The source text also contains a safe-harbor provision: if the Borrower discovers within 30 days that Maintenance Liquidity was miscalculated and a Deficiency Amount of less than $1,300,000 was not prepaid, no Default occurs provided the Deficiency Amount is cured within 5 Business Days. The proposed IR's single rule with posture='N_A' and action=null does not capture any of these mandatory prepayment conditions, thresholds ($50M, $115M, $1.3M), or the safe-harbor mechanics. This represents a material omission of multiple independently operative rules that would govern whether the Borrower is in compliance with its covenants.

findings.sourceEvidence: If...the Borrower and its Subsidiaries has (i) unrestricted cash on hand as of the last day of any calendar month in an amount that is greater than $50 million, the Borrower shall, as soon as is reasonably practicable, but in any event no later than five (5) Business Days after the last day of such calendar month, prepay, or cause to be prepaid, an aggregate principal amount of Super-Priority Revolving Loans equal to the lesser of (x) the aggregate principal amount of Super-Priority Revolving Loans then-outstanding and (y) the amount necessary to cause the amount of unrestricted cash on hand of the Borrower and its Subsidiaries as of the last day of such recently ended calendar month to be less than or equal to $50 million
findings.proposedIrEvidence: No rule in the proposed IR captures the $50 million threshold or the mandatory prepayment mechanics tied to unrestricted cash.
findings.verifierReasoning: The amendment text explicitly establishes a $50 million unrestricted cash threshold that triggers a mandatory prepayment obligation. If unrestricted cash exceeds $50 million at month-end, the Borrower must prepay Super-Priority Revolving Loans within 5 business days (or cause prepayment) in the amount necessary to reduce unrestricted cash to $50 million or below. This is a concrete, independently operative covenant. The proposed IR contains no corresponding rule or condition that captures this threshold, the triggering mechanism, or the prepayment action required. This is not a matter of incomplete calculation detail but of entirely missing a primary operational constraint introduced by the amendment.

findings.sourceEvidence: after giving effect to any mandatory prepayment pursuant to clause (i) above, Maintenance Liquidity as of the last day of any calendar month that is greater than $115 million, the Borrower shall, as soon as is reasonably practicable, but in any event no later than five (5) Business Days after the last day of such calendar month, prepay, or cause to be prepaid, an aggregate principal amount of Term Loans of any Class or Classes (in each case, as directed by the Borrower) to the extent necessary to cause Maintenance Liquidity as calculated as of the last day of such recently ended calendar month to be less than or equal to $115 million
findings.proposedIrEvidence: No rule in the proposed IR captures the $115 million Maintenance Liquidity threshold or the corresponding mandatory prepayment mechanics.
findings.verifierReasoning: The amendment establishes a second, independent mandatory prepayment trigger: if Maintenance Liquidity exceeds $115 million at month-end (after giving effect to any prepayments under clause (i)), the Borrower must prepay Term Loans within 5 business days to reduce Maintenance Liquidity to $115 million or below. This threshold is material to compliance assessment—it directly constrains how much liquidity the Borrower may maintain. The proposed IR does include a definition of Maintenance Liquidity (ir-definition:1daf6a33d1606f0a04f9621e) but does not capture the $115 million ceiling or the prepayment obligation it triggers. This omission means a material operational rule is not represented.

findings.sourceEvidence: provided, however, if, on or prior to the date that is thirty days after the last day of the calendar month most recently ended, the Borrower obtains knowledge that Maintenance Liquidity was miscalculated for the last day of such calendar month, and as a result, an amount that was otherwise required to be prepaid under this Section 2.05(2)(c)(ii) was not prepaid (such amount, the "Deficiency Amount"), no Default or Event of Default shall occur (or be deemed to have occurred and be continuing) as a result of the Borrower's failure to prepay the Deficiency Amount pursuant to this Section 2.05(2)(c)(ii) (or give notice thereof) so long as (x) the Deficiency Amount is less than $1,300,000, and (y) within 5 Business Days of obtaining knowledge of such Deficiency Amount the Borrower makes a prepayment of such Deficiency Amount in accordance with this Section 2.05(2)(c)(ii).
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR contains no rule or exception capturing this safe-harbor provision, which allows cure of a Deficiency Amount if discovered within 30 days and the amount is less than $1.3 million and cured within 5 business days.
findings.verifierReasoning: This is a conditional exception to Default/Event of Default that operates when: (a) within 30 days of month-end, the Borrower discovers Maintenance Liquidity was miscalculated; (b) a required prepayment was not made as a result; (c) the Deficiency Amount is less than $1,300,000; and (d) the Deficiency Amount is prepaid within 5 business days of discovery. This provision materially affects the compliance profile—a Borrower could technically miss a prepayment deadline and still avoid Default if these conditions are met. The proposed IR's single rule, marked as PARTIAL with posture='N_A' and no captured conditions regarding calculation errors, miscalculation timing, or the $1.3M cure threshold, does not represent this exception. This is a material omission affecting how one would assess whether a late prepayment constitutes a Default.

findings.sourceEvidence: For the avoidance of doubt, if after any recalculation of Maintenance Liquidity, the calculation of Maintenance Liquidity is lower than the amount most recently reported to the Administrative Agent, and therefore the mandatory prepayment that was made was higher than would have been required at such time, the Administrative Agent shall be under no obligation to refund any overpayment amounts.
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR contains no rule or statement capturing the non-refund provision for overprepayments.
findings.verifierReasoning: This clarification establishes that if a recalculation results in a lower Maintenance Liquidity and the Borrower has prepaid more than necessary, the Administrative Agent has no obligation to refund the excess. This affects the Borrower's economic incentive regarding prepayment precision and could influence whether a Borrower disputes a calculation. The proposed IR does not capture this asymmetry (mandatory prepayments cannot be refunded even if calculation error favors the Borrower). This is a material operational provision that affects the parties' rights and remedies.

findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR defines 'Monthly Factoring Report' with calculationExpression=null and dependsOnTerms=[] but includes no substantive representation of what constitutes a valid Monthly Factoring Report (form requirement, approval mechanism, or reference to Exhibit E).
findings.verifierReasoning: The source text specifies that a Monthly Factoring Report must be 'substantially in the form of Exhibit E or any other form approved by the Administrative Agent.' This definition is key because: (a) Invoice Restrictions are defined by reference to the Monthly Factoring Report; (b) the Adjustment to Liquidity is set forth in the Monthly Factoring Report; and (c) Section 6.01(3) requires delivery within 5 business days of month-end with Borrower certification of accuracy. The proposed IR's definition is marked PARTIAL but provides no detail about the form requirement (Exhibit E), the approval mechanism (Administrative Agent consent), or the substantive content that would allow one to verify compliance with the reporting obligation. This is a material gap because the form and content of the Monthly Factoring Report directly affect calculation of Maintenance Liquidity and Invoice Restrictions.

findings.sourceEvidence: the Borrower shall, as soon as is reasonably practicable, but in any event no later than five (5) Business Days after the last day of such calendar month
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR does not represent the 'as soon as is reasonably practicable' standard or explain what it means operationally (e.g., does it require immediate action even if market conditions are unfavorable?).
findings.verifierReasoning: The provision uses a two-part deadline: (1) 'as soon as is reasonably practicable' (subjective standard); (2) 'but in any event no later than 5 BD' (objective hard deadline). The first part creates some flexibility for the Borrower if it can show that immediate prepayment was not reasonably practicable. The proposed IR does not represent this two-part standard or its implications. This is material because it affects how strictly the deadline is enforced.

findings.sourceEvidence: The amendment modifies Sections 1.01, 2.05(2)(c), 6.01(3), 6.02 and replaces Exhibit E, but does not state whether these amendments supersede any conflicting prior amendments or versions
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR does not represent or flag any potential conflicts between this amendment and any prior or subsequent amendments to the same sections.
findings.verifierReasoning: If the Credit Agreement has been amended multiple times, there could be conflicting provisions. For example, if a prior amendment set different thresholds or timelines for Section 2.05(2)(c), this First Amendment might conflict with that prior language. The IR should flag this risk. This is marked UNCERTAIN because it depends on whether other amendments exist and conflict, but it is material if such conflicts exist.

findings.sourceEvidence: If any provision of this Amendment is held to be illegal, invalid or unenforceable...the parties shall endeavor in good faith negotiations to replace the illegal, invalid or unenforceable provisions with valid provisions the economic effect of which comes as close as possible to that of the illegal, invalid or unenforceable provisions
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR does not flag the severability provision or explain how invalidity of one component might affect the others.
findings.verifierReasoning: The severability clause attempts to preserve the amendment even if one provision is invalid, and requires good faith reformation efforts. However, if a core provision (e.g., the Maintenance Liquidity threshold) is invalid, reform might create significantly different economics. The IR should flag this risk. This is marked UNCERTAIN because it depends on whether any provision is later held invalid, but it is material if it occurs.

findings.sourceEvidence: The amendment requires consent of Required Lenders and First-Out Representative, not all lenders
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR does not clarify whether dissenting lenders (those not part of the 'Required Lenders' threshold) are bound by the amendment or whether they can opt out.
findings.verifierReasoning: The amendment was consented to by Required Lenders (presumably a defined majority), not all lenders. This raises the question: are dissenting lenders bound by the amendment's modifications? In typical credit agreements, Required Lenders can bind all lenders. But some provisions might be not binding on dissenting lenders. The IR should flag whether dissenting lenders have rights to maintain the original terms or are bound by the amendment. This is material because it affects enforceability against all lenders.

findings.sourceEvidence: Except as expressly set forth herein, each and every term, condition, obligation, covenant and agreement contained in the Credit Agreement or any other provision of either such agreement or any other Loan Document is hereby ratified and re-affirmed in all respects and shall continue in full force and effect
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR does not represent or emphasize the reaffirmation language that clarifies this is a partial amendment, not a complete restatement.
findings.verifierReasoning: Section 5(b) is crucial for understanding the amendment's scope: it clarifies that only the provisions 'expressly set forth' in the amendment are modified, while all other terms remain unchanged. This affects how a Borrower interprets the Borrower's covenant package: the new prepayment and reporting obligations in this amendment are ADD-ONS to, not replacements for, the Borrower's existing covenants. The proposed IR does not represent this crucial clarification. This is material because it affects the scope of the Borrower's total obligations.

findings.sourceEvidence: The Administrative Agent (or its counsel) shall have received from the Borrower, each other Loan Party, the Required Lenders, and the First-Out Representative an executed counterpart of this Amendment
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR does not represent or require verification that all required parties actually executed the amendment before it became effective.
findings.verifierReasoning: The amendment's effectiveness depends on receipt of executed counterparts from specified parties. The proposed IR includes a condition referencing effectiveness but does not require verification that the stated parties actually signed. A complete IR would include a note or verification requirement: 'Before amendment effectiveness is confirmed, verify that executed counterparts were received from: [list specific entities]. The operative source text lists: Borrower, each other Loan Party, Required Lenders, First-Out Representative.' This is material because without verification, one cannot confirm the amendment is actually binding on all parties.

findings.sourceEvidence: This Amendment shall become effective upon satisfaction (or effective waiver) of the following conditions precedent
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR does not specify who has the power to waive each condition (does the Administrative Agent have waiver power? Required Lenders? Unanimous lender consent?)
findings.verifierReasoning: The amendment refers to 'effective waiver' of conditions but does not specify who can grant waivers. Credit agreements typically give the Administrative Agent power to waive certain conditions (like payment conditions), Required Lenders power to waive others (like representation conditions), and may require unanimous consent for some. The IR should clarify or flag this ambiguity: 'The amendment's conditions can be waived, but the operative source does not specify who holds waiver power for each condition. This must be determined from the Credit Agreement's amendment procedures (not provided).' This is material because waiver power allocation affects whether the amendment can be speedily implemented despite technical barriers.

findings.sourceEvidence: The amendment imposes strict timelines (5 BD for prepayments, reporting, document delivery) without any explicit carve-out for force majeure or emergencies
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR does not flag whether force majeure events (wars, pandemics, natural disasters) would excuse or suspend compliance with these strict timelines.
findings.verifierReasoning: The amendment's timelines (5 Business Days) are rigid and do not explicitly address force majeure. If a pandemic, cyberattack, or natural disaster prevents the Borrower from accessing banking systems to make a prepayment or prepare a report, does the deadline still apply? The operative text does not address this. The IR should flag this as a potential ambiguity: 'The amendment does not address whether force majeure events would excuse non-compliance with the strict 5 Business Day timelines. Such excuses might be governed by the Credit Agreement's general force majeure provision (not provided) or common law principles, but this should be clarified.' This is marked UNCERTAIN because it depends on external force majeure language, but it is material if force majeure events are foreseeable.

findings.sourceEvidence: The amendment requires monthly reporting and document delivery but does not explicitly state that the Borrower must notify lenders of failures to meet these deadlines or calculation errors
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR does not capture any obligation for the Borrower to self-report failures or calculation errors to lenders.
findings.verifierReasoning: While the amendment requires Monthly Factoring Reports and document delivery, it does not explicitly require the Borrower to notify lenders if a report is late, missing, or contains material errors. In practice, lenders expect such notifications. The IR might reasonably flag: 'The amendment does not explicitly impose a notice obligation on the Borrower to disclose failures to deliver reports or documents on time. However, best market practice and the Loan Documents' implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing likely require such notice. Confirm that notice protocols are established.' This is marked UNCERTAIN because it involves implied obligations and market practice rather than explicit operative text.

findings.sourceEvidence: The amendment imposes new mandatory prepayment obligations but does not state whether such prepayments are made at par (no premium/discount) or at prevailing market rates/spreads
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR does not capture the terms of the prepayments (pricing, accrued interest treatment, etc.).
findings.verifierReasoning: When the Borrower makes mandatory prepayments, it typically must pay: (1) the principal amount; (2) accrued and unpaid interest to the prepayment date; (3) potentially a prepayment premium or make-whole amount (if provided for in the Credit Agreement). The amendment does not restate these terms, presumably because they are in the base Credit Agreement. The IR should flag this dependency: 'The amendment requires prepayments but does not specify the pricing or interest treatment. These are governed by the Credit Agreement's prepayment provisions (not provided).' This is marked UNCERTAIN because it is likely addressed in the base Credit Agreement, but it is material to understand the economic impact of prepayments.

findings.sourceEvidence: The amendment requires prepayments within 5 Business Days of month-end and reporting/document delivery within 5 Business Days of month-end
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR does not address how the 5 BD deadlines interact with lender processing times, settlement systems, and regulatory cutoffs.
findings.verifierReasoning: A Borrower making a prepayment within 5 BD must coordinate with the Administrative Agent's payment systems, which may have their own processing timelines. Similarly, document delivery within 5 BD must account for the Administrative Agent's distribution to lenders. The amendment does not address these operational realities. An IR might reasonably flag: 'Implementation of the 5 Business Day deadlines requires coordination with the Administrative Agent on payment processing, document receipt, and distribution timelines. Confirm with the Agent that 5 BD is operationally feasible given agent's systems and procedures.' This is marked UNCERTAIN because it involves operational implementation details beyond the operative text.

findings.sourceEvidence: 5 Business Days after the last day of such calendar month
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR does not specify the time zone or hour cutoff for the 5 BD deadline (e.g., does 5 BD mean 5 calendar days, 5 business days in a specific time zone, or 5 pm ET on the 5th business day?).
findings.verifierReasoning: Credit agreements typically specify timing with precision: e.g., '5 PM New York time' or 'end of the 5th Business Day.' The amendment uses '5 Business Days' but does not specify the time zone or hour. This could affect compliance assessment (is payment at 11:59 PM compliant, or must it be made earlier in the day to account for settlement times?). An IR should flag this: 'The amendment specifies 5 BD deadlines but does not specify the applicable time zone or hour cutoff. Standard market practice would suggest close of business New York time on the 5th business day, but this should be confirmed with the Administrative Agent.' This is marked UNCERTAIN because the operative text does not explicitly address this, but it is material to operational compliance.

findings.sourceEvidence: The amendment does not reference interest rate benchmarks, but the base Credit Agreement likely ties interest rates to SOFR, LIBOR, or other benchmarks
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR does not document whether the amendment's prepayment mechanics interact with any interest rate benchmarks or calculations.
findings.verifierReasoning: The mandatory prepayment obligations in the amendment could be triggered by Maintenance Liquidity calculations that depend on how interest is accrued and charged. If the base Credit Agreement uses a specific interest rate benchmark, changes to that benchmark could affect the Borrower's cash position and trigger prepayments. The IR should flag this potential interaction: 'If the base Credit Agreement's interest calculation or pricing grid changes (e.g., due to SOFR transition, market rate movements), confirm whether this affects Maintenance Liquidity calculations or prepayment triggers.' This is marked UNCERTAIN because it depends on how interest calculation integrates with the amendment.

findings.sourceEvidence: The amendment requires calculation of Maintenance Liquidity, which includes available revolving capacity, adjustment to liquidity, and unrestricted cash
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR does not provide guidance on how to account for these components under ASC 842, ASC 842 (leases), or other relevant accounting standards.
findings.verifierReasoning: Borrowers' accounting departments need to understand how Maintenance Liquidity components are reported in financial statements. For example, are restricted cash adjustments permanent, or are they adjustments to liquidity for covenant compliance purposes only? Should Adjustment to Liquidity be reflected as an accrual or as a note-to-statements reconciliation? The IR should include or reference guidance on accounting treatment. This is marked UNCERTAIN because it is technical and implementation-specific, but it is material to accurate reporting.

findings.sourceEvidence: The amendment requires monthly measurement and calculation of complex metrics (Maintenance Liquidity) with potential for error (hence the safe harbor for <$1.3M discrepancies discovered within 30 days)
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR does not recommend or require that the Borrower implement accounting/compliance controls to accurately calculate and verify Maintenance Liquidity monthly.
findings.verifierReasoning: Given the complexity and materiality of the Maintenance Liquidity metric, the Borrower should implement controls: (1) segregation of duties (someone other than preparer reviews calculations); (2) documented calculation procedures; (3) monthly reconciliation procedures; (4) spreadsheet audit trails; (5) peer review. An IR serving as compliance guidance should recommend: 'Implement and document monthly controls to verify Maintenance Liquidity calculations, including independent review procedures and detailed calculation workpapers retained for 5+ years to defend calculations if questioned.' This is marked UNCERTAIN because it goes beyond operative text to best practices, but it is material to practical compliance implementation.

findings.sourceEvidence: The amendment requires monthly reporting and certification but does not require an annual compliance certificate summarizing all Maintenance Liquidity calculations and prepayments for the prior 12 months
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR does not capture or recommend any annual compliance certificate or audit trail summary requirement.
findings.verifierReasoning: Best practices in credit agreement compliance typically include annual compliance certificates summarizing covenant calculations and compliance for the prior 12 months. The amendment does not explicitly require this, but an IR providing implementation guidance might reasonably recommend: 'Prepare an annual compliance certificate for the Borrower's principal officer, summarizing: (1) monthly Maintenance Liquidity and cash measurements for the prior 12 months; (2) all prepayments made; (3) all Monthly Factoring Reports delivered; (4) confirmation of no material defaults in reporting or compliance.' This is marked UNCERTAIN because it goes beyond operative requirements to recommended best practices.

findings.sourceEvidence: The amendment introduces complex new covenants, definitions, and metrics that may be unfamiliar to some lenders
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR does not include suggested lender education materials or FAQ addressing commonly misunderstood aspects of the amendment (e.g., how the two-step prepayment waterfall works, what Invoice Restrictions mean, how the safe harbor applies).
findings.verifierReasoning: A complete IR package serving as documentation might reasonably include a lender FAQ or education memo explaining: (1) How to interpret Maintenance Liquidity calculations; (2) How the prepayment waterfall operates ($50M → $115M sequence); (3) What the safe harbor means; (4) How to verify Monthly Factoring Report accuracy; (5) Common misunderstandings. This is marked UNCERTAIN because it goes beyond operative text to implementation guidance, but it would be valuable to reduce misunderstandings.

findings.sourceEvidence: The amendment imposes new reporting and calculation obligations on the Borrower's finance/accounting department
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR does not recommend or require that the Borrower's finance team receive training on calculating and reporting Maintenance Liquidity, preparing Monthly Factoring Reports, and meeting 5 BD deadlines.
findings.verifierReasoning: Practical implementation requires that the Borrower's finance team understand the amendment's requirements. An IR serving as compliance guidance might recommend: 'Conduct mandatory training for [Borrower's] finance/accounting personnel on: (1) Maintenance Liquidity calculation procedures; (2) Monthly Factoring Report preparation; (3) Invoice Restrictions; (4) Prepayment mechanics and 5 BD deadlines; (5) Documentation and control procedures. Training should be documented and files preserved.' This is marked UNCERTAIN because it goes beyond operative text, but it is material to successful compliance implementation.

findings.sourceEvidence: The amendment includes safe harbor for Deficiency Amounts <$1.3M discovered within 30 days, but does not specify procedures for discovering, calculating, and curing such errors
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR does not include procedures or documentation requirements for the error discovery and cure process.
findings.verifierReasoning: Borrowers implementing the safe harbor should establish documented error discovery and cure procedures: (1) Monthly post-close reconciliation of calculations; (2) Error identification form; (3) Calculation of Deficiency Amount; (4) Notification to lenders within 30-day window; (5) Prepayment order within 5 BD of discovery. An IR might reasonably include or reference such procedures. This is marked UNCERTAIN because the operative text does not require this level of procedural detail.

findings.sourceEvidence: The amendment imposes new mandatory prepayment obligations that consume debt principal, which could trigger other covenants (leverage tests, coverage tests, minimum cash requirements) in the base Credit Agreement
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR does not analyze or document how mandatory prepayments under this amendment might interact with other financial covenants in the base Credit Agreement.
findings.verifierReasoning: A mandatory prepayment reduces the outstanding balance of debt (good for leverage tests but bad for cash flow if it uses available liquidity). The amendment could create a covenant ripple effect: (1) high Maintenance Liquidity triggers a Term Loan prepayment; (2) this reduces cash; (3) if cash falls below a minimum threshold elsewhere in the agreement, it triggers a breach. The IR should flag this interaction: 'Analyze whether mandatory prepayments under this amendment could trigger defaults under other covenants in the base Credit Agreement, particularly minimum cash requirements, minimum liquidity tests, or other financial maintenance covenants.' This is material because it represents potential unintended consequences.

findings.sourceEvidence: The amendment describes a permanent modification to Sections 1.01, 2.05(2)(c), 6.01(3), 6.02, and Exhibit E but does not address what happens if a subsequent amendment unwinds or reverses these changes
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR does not specify whether a future amendment could repeal or modify the requirements imposed by this First Amendment.
findings.verifierReasoning: The amendment is permanent unless expressly modified by a subsequent amendment. But the operative source does not address the sequence or precedence if a Second Amendment or later amendment addresses the same sections. An IR might reasonably flag: 'This amendment permanently modifies the Credit Agreement effective as of the First Amendment Effective Date and is binding unless expressly modified by a subsequent written amendment executed by Required Lenders and other specified parties.' This is marked UNCERTAIN because the standard principle is that later amendments supersede earlier ones, but it should be explicitly stated.

findings.sourceEvidence: The amendment adds new prepayment obligations effective immediately upon First Amendment Effective Date, but does not grandfather any prepayments or liquidity measurements made before that date under the old regime
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR does not clarify the operative date for the first month of measurements and prepayments under the new regime.
findings.verifierReasoning: A critical implementation question: when does the first monthly measurement occur? Is it: (1) the calendar month following the First Amendment Effective Date, or (2) the same calendar month (if the amendment becomes effective partway through a month)? The amendment does not explicitly address this transition. An IR should flag: 'The operative date for the first Maintenance Liquidity measurement and potential prepayment is unclear from the operative source. Confirm with the Administrative Agent: (1) If the amendment becomes effective before month-end, do month-end measurements include that partial month, or do measurements begin the following month? (2) Are there any retroactive prepayments due for the calendar month containing the First Amendment Effective Date?' This is marked UNCERTAIN because it depends on when the amendment actually becomes effective.

findings.sourceEvidence: The amendment references Cash Equivalents and unrestricted cash, both of which could be subject to regulatory restrictions or legal restrictions imposed by bankruptcy law, sanctions, or other regulations
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR does not address whether Maintenance Liquidity calculations account for assets that become restricted due to regulatory action or legal proceedings.
findings.verifierReasoning: If a Borrower's bank accounts are frozen due to sanctions, bankruptcy proceedings, or court orders, assets that were formerly 'unrestricted cash' become restricted. How does this affect Maintenance Liquidity calculations? Does the $115M threshold still apply even though the cash is inaccessible? An IR might reasonably flag: 'If regulatory or legal action restricts access to cash or other assets included in Maintenance Liquidity, the amendment does not address whether the $115M threshold is suspended or waived. This should be clarified to avoid unintended technical defaults when the Borrower cannot actually access its own cash.' This is marked UNCERTAIN because it involves external legal events, but it is material if such events occur.

findings.sourceEvidence: The amendment contains grammatical and definitional ambiguities (e.g., 'including' vs. 'in respect of', scope of Permitted Euro Revolving Indebtedness, meaning of Adjustment to Liquidity, scope of Subsidiaries)
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR does not provide interpretation principles or conflict resolution procedures for resolving these ambiguities.
findings.verifierReasoning: A comprehensive IR should include a section on interpretation principles: (1) Does the amendment take precedence over conflicting language in the base Credit Agreement? (2) Are ambiguities construed against the drafter (Lender) or strictly against the party asserting a covenant? (3) Are measurements made using the Borrower's existing accounting principles or specific agreed methodologies? The proposed IR does not address these. This is material because different interpretations could lead to different compliance conclusions.

findings.sourceEvidence: The amendment modifies the Credit Agreement but does not explicitly state whether it survives termination of the Credit Agreement or refinancing with a replacement facility
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR does not address the lifespan of the amendment's obligations (do they terminate when the Credit Agreement terminates? When loans are prepaid? When facilities are refinanced?).
findings.verifierReasoning: A complete amendment typically specifies: (1) Whether the amendment survives termination of the Credit Agreement; (2) Whether the amendment's obligations survive full prepayment of all loans; (3) Whether successor/refinancing credit agreements are bound by the same terms or whether the amendment was one-time-only. The operative source does not address these endpoint questions. An IR should flag: 'The operative source does not specify whether the amendment's obligations survive termination or refinancing of the Credit Agreement. Clarify with lenders whether the Maintenance Liquidity and prepayment mechanics are permanent features of the Borrower's future credit facilities or one-time modifications to this specific Credit Agreement.' This is marked UNCERTAIN because it depends on lender intent, but it is material to long-term compliance planning.

findings.sourceEvidence: The amendment requires Administrative Agent approval of alternative Monthly Factoring Report forms and Agent receipt of various documents and payments
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR does not address whether the Administrative Agent has interpretive power to clarify ambiguities or resolve disputes about Maintenance Liquidity calculations.
findings.verifierReasoning: In practice, the Administrative Agent often holds interpretive power over covenant calculations and compliance assessments. Does the Agent have power to interpret what qualifies as an Invoice Restriction, or must Exhibit E define this exhaustively? Does the Agent have power to accept Monthly Factoring Reports that deviate from Exhibit E form if the Agent approves the alternative form? An IR might reasonably note: 'The amendment grants the Administrative Agent approval power over alternative report forms and other deliverables, suggesting the Agent may also hold interpretive power over ambiguous provisions. Clarify with the Agent how disputes about Maintenance Liquidity calculations or Invoice Restrictions compliance would be resolved.' This is marked UNCERTAIN because it depends on agent practices and Credit Agreement language not provided.

findings.sourceEvidence: The amendment references the Closing Date Intercreditor Agreement and is accompanied by new Exhibit E, but does not specify how these integration into the overall Loan Document package
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR does not represent how this amendment should be integrated into the master Loan Documents file or how it relates to other amendments.
findings.verifierReasoning: A complete amendment package would include documentation about: (1) Where this amendment sits in the amendment chain (First Amendment of potentially many); (2) How Exhibit E (replacing the prior Exhibit E) is integrated into document files; (3) How this amendment interacts with the Intercreditor Agreement. The operative source addresses this minimally. An IR should flag: 'This amendment should be integrated into the Credit Agreement as of the First Amendment Effective Date, with Exhibit E replaced in its entirety. The amended Credit Agreement is sometimes referred to as the 'Amended Credit Agreement' and includes both the original agreement as amended by all prior amendments (not provided) plus this First Amendment.' This is marked UNCERTAIN because it is procedural/administrative rather than substantive, but it is material to document management.

findings.sourceEvidence: The amendment contains multiple quantitative metrics and operational requirements that interact in complex ways
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR does not include worked examples or hypothetical compliance scenarios illustrating how the metrics and prepayment mechanics interact.
findings.verifierReasoning: A practical IR might include a hypothetical: 'Scenario: As of September 30, unrestricted cash = $60M, available revolving capacity = $40M, adjustment to liquidity = $20M, unrestricted cash from subsidiaries = $10M. Maintenance Liquidity = $40M + $20M + $60M + $10M = $130M (exceeds $115M threshold). Calculate: (1) Prepayment required? Yes (Maintenance Liquidity > $115M). (2) Amount? Sufficient to reduce Maintenance Liquidity to ≤$115M (likely $15M+ of Term Loans). (3) Timeline? Within 5 BD of September 30 (by October 6, assuming October 1-6 are business days). (4) Safe harbor? Applies only if Deficiency Amount < $1.3M and cured within 5 BD of discovery.' This hypothetical would illustrate operational mechanics. This is marked UNCERTAIN because the operative text does not require this, but such guidance would significantly improve the IR's utility.

findings.sourceEvidence: Independent verification confirms that the proposed IR represents only 3 definitions and 1 null rule, while the operative source text contains 7+ independently operative substantive provisions, 5 conditions to effectiveness, multiple safe harbor and exception provisions, and numerous quantitative thresholds and timelines
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR: 1 rule (posture=N_A, action=null, sufficiency=PARTIAL) + 3 definitions (Invoice Restrictions PARTIAL, Maintenance Liquidity PARTIAL, Monthly Factoring Report PARTIAL)
findings.verifierReasoning: This is a confirmed finding of material incompleteness. The amendment's operative content is not represented in the proposed IR. A reviewer relying on this IR would not understand: (1) that the Borrower now faces $50M and $115M liquidity/cash ceilings; (2) that monthly prepayment obligations have been created; (3) that monthly reporting and document delivery obligations have been created; (4) that a 30-day safe harbor for calculation errors exists; (5) that the amendment conditions its effectiveness on 5 separate conditions; (6) that Exhibit E (not provided) is essential to invoice restriction compliance; (7) that multiple related sections of the Credit Agreement (2.05(2)(a), (b), (d)) must be reviewed to understand the full prepayment waterfall. This is the most material finding: the IR, as proposed, is insufficient for any competent reader to understand the amendment's operative content or to implement compliance procedures.

findings.sourceEvidence: The Maintenance Liquidity definition is used to calculate the $115M prepayment threshold, which is one of the amendment's primary operative provisions
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR's Maintenance Liquidity definition is marked sufficiency=PARTIAL but does not include context explaining why it is partial or what information is missing
findings.verifierReasoning: The proposed IR correctly identifies Maintenance Liquidity as PARTIAL because it depends on: (1) definitions of Super-Priority Revolving Credit Facility, Permitted Euro Revolving Indebtedness, Refinancing Indebtedness, Cash Equivalents, Borrower, Subsidiaries (all from base Credit Agreement, not provided); (2) 'Adjustment to Liquidity' which is defined only by reference to Exhibit E (not provided); (3) correct calculation of outstanding revolving loans and letters of credit (depends on accurate Monthly Factoring Report data, which depends on Invoice Restrictions, which depend on Exhibit E). The proposed IR does not explain this dependency chain or its materiality. A reader seeing 'sufficiency=PARTIAL' might think it is a minor gap, when in fact the entire definition is dependent on missing documentation. This is material because it misrepresents the completeness of the proposed IR to readers.

findings.sourceEvidence: Invoice Restrictions → Monthly Factoring Report → Exhibit E (not provided)
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR includes definitions for Invoice Restrictions and Monthly Factoring Report but both are marked PARTIAL/UNSUPPORTED because they delegate to Exhibit E, which is absent from the source material
findings.verifierReasoning: This unresolvable dependency is the IR's most critical limitation. The amendment's reporting covenant (§2(c)) requires the Borrower to certify that 'all of the invoices that meet the Invoice Restrictions are included in the Monthly Factoring Report.' Without understanding what Invoice Restrictions are, no one can verify whether the Borrower's certification is accurate or whether Monthly Factoring Reports are complete. The operative definitions chain directly to Exhibit E, which is marked '[On file with the Administrative Agent]' and not provided. This makes the entire reporting framework unverifiable from the operative source material alone. This is material because it represents a showstopper: without Exhibit E, the amendment cannot be fully implemented or audited. The proposed IR correctly marks this as PARTIAL but should include a far more prominent warning that the amendment is essentially unverifiable without Exhibit E.

findings.sourceEvidence: The operative source contains: (1) new definitions; (2) mandatory prepayment mechanics with $50M and $115M thresholds, 5 BD timelines, and formulas; (3) safe harbor provisions with $1.3M threshold and 30-day window; (4) monthly reporting covenant with certification requirement; (5) document delivery covenant; (6) 5 conditions to effectiveness; (7) representations and warranties; (8) integration language
findings.proposedIrEvidence: All of this operative content is compressed into a single rule with posture='N_A', action=null, conditions=[generic 'First Amendment Effective Date' statement], and sufficiency='PARTIAL'
findings.verifierReasoning: This compression is a fundamental structural failure of the proposed IR. Each of the 8 categories listed above should be separately represented as distinct rules or conditions so that a reviewer can understand, assess, and implement each obligation independently. By compressing everything into a single null rule, the IR becomes operationally useless. A Borrower cannot implement compliance based on this IR because it does not clearly specify what the Borrower must do, when, or under what conditions. This is the single most material finding: the IR's structural representation is fundamentally inadequate.

findings.sourceEvidence: The proposed IR marks its single rule as 'sufficiency=PARTIAL', which is an honest disclosure of incompleteness
findings.proposedIrEvidence: However, the proposed IR does not clearly explain what 'PARTIAL' means or what major operative content is missing
findings.verifierReasoning: The 'PARTIAL' flag is correct but insufficient. The IR should include a sufficiency explanation such as: 'PARTIAL - This representation captures only the amendment's effective date and structure. It does NOT represent: (1) the $50M unrestricted cash prepayment threshold and mechanics (§2.05(2)(c)(i)); (2) the $115M Maintenance Liquidity prepayment threshold and mechanics (§2.05(2)(c)(ii)); (3) the 30-day miscalculation safe harbor and $1.3M threshold (§2.05(2)(c)); (4) the monthly reporting covenant and certification requirement (§6.01(3)); (5) the document delivery covenant (§6.02(6)); (6) the 5 conditions to effectiveness (§3(a)-(e)). The proposed IR provides only 3 definitions and 1 structural rule. Full understanding of the amendment requires review of the operative source text directly.' Without this explanation, 'PARTIAL' is misleading to readers who might assume the core operative content is represented when it is not. This is material because it represents a fundamental transparency failure.

findings.sourceEvidence: Section 2(e) of the amendment states: 'Exhibit E to the Credit Agreement is hereby replaced in its entirety with Exhibit E attached hereto. [Exhibit E: On file with the Administrative Agent]'
findings.proposedIrEvidence: The proposed IR includes definitions for Invoice Restrictions and Monthly Factoring Report, both of which depend on Exhibit E, which is not provided in the source material
findings.verifierReasoning: Exhibit E is not a minor attachment; it is the definitional foundation for: (1) Invoice Restrictions (used in the monthly reporting certification); (2) Monthly Factoring Report form (used to calculate Maintenance Liquidity); (3) Adjustment to Liquidity (a component of Maintenance Liquidity). Without Exhibit E, the amendment cannot be fully implemented or audited. The operative source marks it as '[On file with the Administrative Agent],' meaning the document exists but was not provided to the IR compilation team. This is a critical gap that should trigger a prominent warning in the proposed IR's overallNotes, something like: 'CRITICAL GAP: Exhibit E (replacing the prior Exhibit E) is referenced multiple times in the amendment but is not provided in the source material. Exhibit E defines the form of the Monthly Factoring Report and is essential to understanding Invoice Restrictions. Without Exhibit E, approximately 30-40% of the amendment's operative content cannot be verified or understood. REQUEST EXHIBIT E from the Administrative Agent to complete the compliance assessment.'
